ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: The figure below is a double-reciprocal plot of one of the three types of reversible inhibition of enzymes; please determine which type of inhibition this is. \begin{center} \includegraphics[scale=0.5]{q_00349_001.png} \end{center}
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: The figure is a double-reciprocal plot of enzyme kinetics, with the vertical axis labeled 1/v and the horizontal axis labeled 1/[S]. Several straight lines pass through the same vertical-axis intercept, labeled beside it as 1/Vmax; on the right there is an arrow labeled “[I] increases,” indicating that when the inhibitor concentration increases, the slope of the straight lines gradually becomes larger. The slope of the straight line under normal conditions is smaller; as [I] increases, the negative intercept on the horizontal axis moves from -1/Km toward -1/[Km(1+[I]/Ki)] close to the origin. Then reason: In the double-reciprocal plot, the vertical-axis intercept 1/Vmax is unchanged, indicating that Vmax is unchanged; the slope increases and the horizontal-axis intercept approaches the origin, indicating that the apparent Km increases. This is exactly the characteristic of competitive inhibition.

planner_metadata.image_role: Read the plotted axes as 1/v versus 1/[S]. Observe that the normal line and the lines with increasing inhibitor concentration [I] all intersect at the same y-intercept labeled 1/Vmax, while their slopes increase and the x-intercept shifts from -1/Km toward -1/(Km(1+[I]/Ki)).
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question statement that the figure is one of the three reversible enzyme inhibition Lineweaver–Burk plots and asks for the inhibition type.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: In a Lineweaver–Burk plot, competitive inhibition leaves Vmax unchanged, so the y-intercept 1/Vmax is constant, but increases apparent Km, so the slope increases and the x-intercept changes. Noncompetitive and uncompetitive inhibition have different intercept patterns.
